introduction: These passages tell of the banishment of Bahá’u’lláh from Constantinople to Adrianople in the winter of 1863 and of the five years there: the crowded room and the joy of the exiles, the cold of the road, the withdrawal that separated the faithful from the faithless, the letters to the kings, the respect of the townspeople, and the sudden order that sent the company on to Acre. They return often to one thought: each exile, meant to end the cause, spread it. Each of the twenty-one quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Paul and Silas singing in prison, Ruth's 'whither thou goest', the spoiling of goods borne joyfully, the church scattered and so spread, Joseph's 'God meant it unto good'. Three push back or add a side: the exiles who wept by the rivers of Babylon, Machiavelli on unarmed prophets, and Voltaire on calling calamity a blessing.
questions: More than fifteen people lived in one room and were 'filled with joy and composure'. The exiles in Babylon wept. What makes the difference?
The readings say that each banishment strengthened the cause it was meant to end. Where else in history has that happened, and where has it not?
From Adrianople letters went out to kings. What does it mean to address the powerful from a place of exile?
When the order came to leave, the exiles' goods were seized and their destination hidden from them. What do the readings ask us to learn from how they bore it?

outside.why: Acts tells how Paul and Silas, in prison at midnight, prayed and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them.
The exiles in Babylon sat down and wept, and asked how they should sing the Lord's song in a strange land. What makes one company of exiles weep and another, crowded into a single room, speak of joy?
The letter to the Hebrews says: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Jesus says to one who would follow him: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Ruth says to Naomi: whither thou goest, I will go, and where thou lodgest, I will lodge.
Matthew says that the people were astonished at Jesus's teaching, for he taught them as one having authority.
Lovelace wrote from prison that stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage.
Mark tells how Jesus rose a great while before day, departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
On Carmel Elijah stood alone before the people and the prophets of Baal, and the fire of the Lord fell.
The psalm addresses rulers: be wise now therefore, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Paul writes from prison that the things which happened unto him have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.
Paul writes: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
The letter to the Hebrews reminds its readers that they took joyfully the spoiling of their goods.
Jesus tells his disciples to pray that their flight be not in the winter.
Acts tells how a great persecution scattered the church abroad throughout Judaea and Samaria.
Gamaliel warns the council: if this work be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.

Machiavelli concluded from history that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. What does the story of four exiles, each of which strengthened the cause, do to his rule?
Joseph says to the brothers who sold him: ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good.
Paul writes that all things work together for good to them that love God.

Voltaire asked, after an earthquake, whether a general bliss can be composed from individuals' woes. To whom is it fitting to say that a calamity was in reality a bounty: to the one who suffered it, or only about him?
Job, stripped of all he had, says: naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither.

matthew-flight-not-in-the-winter.text: But pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day

luke-foxes-have-holes.text: And it came to pass, that, as they went in the way, a certain man said unto him, Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest. And Jesus said unto him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head
